::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This guide goes with [meeting 11](../sessions/11-figures.qmd). Use it
in session B to critique figures, and run it on every figure in your
proposal, due December 11, and on every figure in your final
presentation.
:::

A figure made for a reader shows one comparison. It is built in four
steps, and each step asks four questions. A figure that fails a
question in step 1 or step 4 leaves the reader without the message. A
figure that fails a question in step 2 is read imprecisely, and one
that fails in step 3 is read with a bias: the reader comes away
believing something the numbers do not say.

Figures you make to explore your own data do not need any of this.
Make many, quickly, and look at every one before you fit a model
(meeting 5). This guide is for the few you show.

## 1. Choose the comparison

| | Question | What goes wrong | What to do |
|:-|:-----|:---------|:---------|
| 1.1 | What is the message, in one sentence? | Everything is shown and nothing is compared | Write the message before drawing, then draw only its comparison |
| 1.2 | Compared with what? | A change shown with no comparison group or no period before it | Add the comparison group and the period before the change |
| 1.3 | Which quantity shows it? | Nominal dollars, levels, two series or counts when the message needs real dollars, growth, the gap or a rate | Deflate money by a price index; index to a base year; plot the gap; divide by the population |
| 1.4 | Which form shows it? | A bar of means hides the distribution; a figure holds numbers a reader needs to look up | Show the data points or the distribution; put exact values in a table |

To find a chart form for a comparison, look the comparison up in the
Financial Times [Visual
Vocabulary](https://github.com/Financial-Times/chart-doctor/tree/main/visual-vocabulary):
deviation, correlation, ranking, distribution, change over time,
magnitude, part-to-whole, spatial or flow.

## 2. Encode it for the eye

Readers judge positions on a common scale more accurately than
lengths, angles, areas or colors ([Cleveland and McGill
1984](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1984.10478080); [Heer and Bostock
2010](https://doi.org/10.1145/1753326.1753357)).

| | Question | What goes wrong | What to do |
|:-|:-----|:---------|:---------|
| 2.1 | Is the key comparison on a common scale? | A pie, a stacked bar or bubbles make close values hard to rank | Put the values on one axis as dots or bars, sorted |
| 2.2 | Does the channel match the data? | A rainbow color scale for ordered values; lines joining categories that have no order | Use one hue, light to dark, for ordered values; use lines only for time or another ordered axis |
| 2.3 | Are the compared items next to each other? | Many series tangled in one panel; compared groups on separate panels with different scales | Draw small multiples on shared axes; put compared groups side by side on one scale |
| 2.4 | Do the points hide each other? | Thousands of points overplotted into a blot | Make the points transparent and add the mean of y within bins of x (a binned scatter) |

## 3. Keep it faithful

| | Question | What goes wrong | What to do |
|:-|:-----|:---------|:---------|
| 3.1 | Does the scale match the quantity? | A bar axis that skips zero; a log scale the reader takes for linear; an inverted axis; circles scaled by radius; 3D | Start bars at zero; use a linear scale for a general reader; scale circles by area; draw in 2D |
| 3.2 | Do the window and the sample favor the message? | Two y-axes whose ranges set where the lines cross; a time window that starts where the story looks best; a total that hides opposite subgroups; a sample that loses its failures over time | Put compared series on one scale; show the full period or say why the window starts where it does; show the subgroups; say who left the sample |
| 3.3 | Is the uncertainty shown? | Point estimates with no intervals; error bars that do not say what they are | Draw 95% confidence intervals and say so in the caption; do not read overlapping intervals as no difference |
| 3.4 | Does the title claim only what the figure shows? | A causal title on a correlation | Title the association; leave causal claims to a design (meetings 8 and 9) |

## 4. Finish it for the reader

Show the data, reduce the clutter, and integrate the text and the
graph ([Schwabish 2014](https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.28.1.209)).

| | Question | What goes wrong | What to do |
|:-|:-----|:---------|:---------|
| 4.1 | Does the title state the finding? | A label title ("Sales by region, 2020–2025") | Write the finding as the title; put the variables in a subtitle or the axis titles |
| 4.2 | Does every mark carry information? | Heavy gridlines, borders, shading, markers, a legend of codes, variable names as axis titles | Delete what carries no data; label lines where they end; write units in the axis titles; color one thing and leave the rest grey |
| 4.3 | Does the caption let the figure stand alone? | "Figure 3: Effects" | Give the source, the unit, the sample, the estimator and what the error bars are |
| 4.4 | Does it fit the page or the slide? | A paper's four-panel figure on a slide; red against green | Redraw for the slide with one panel and large type; use a palette color-blind readers can tell apart, such as Okabe–Ito ([Wong 2011](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.1618)) |

Across a document, the same group keeps the same color in every
figure.

## Checklist before you submit

- [ ] Each figure's message fits in one sentence, and that sentence is
  its title.
- [ ] Each figure that shows a change also shows a comparison group or
  the period before.
- [ ] Money over time is in real dollars, with the base year stated.
- [ ] No bar chart has an axis that skips zero.
- [ ] No two series share a figure on two different y-axes.
- [ ] Every estimate has its interval, and the caption says which
  interval.
- [ ] No title claims a cause the design cannot support.
- [ ] Every axis title has its unit, and no axis title is a variable
  name.
- [ ] Every caption gives the source, the sample and the unit.
- [ ] Every slide figure has one panel and type the back row can read.

## Further reading

- Schwabish (2014), "[An economist's guide to visualizing
  data](https://doi.org/10.1257/jep.28.1.209)", *Journal of Economic
  Perspectives*. Short, free, and written for economists, with eight
  published figures redrawn.
- Wilke (2019), [*Fundamentals of Data
  Visualization*](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/), free online.
  Organized by what you want to show.
- Healy (2018), [*Data Visualization: A Practical
  Introduction*](https://socviz.co), free online, with R code.
- Zelazny (2001), *Say It With Charts*, 4th edition, McGraw-Hill. How
  to choose a chart from its message.
- Franconeri, Padilla, Shah, Zacks and Hullman (2021), "[The science of
  visual data communication: what
  works](https://doi.org/10.1177/15291006211051956)", *Psychological
  Science in the Public Interest*. The experiments behind these rules.
